claims.text: The stable-to-unstable wear transition in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is driven by a temperature-induced reduction in stacking-fault energy.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating is equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating has an FCC solid-solution structure at 300 K.
The coating has a nanocrystalline or fine-grained microstructure.
The initial coating contains a high dislocation density and stable stacking faults.
Nanoindentation and sliding friction are applied while temperature is increased from 300 K to 600 K.
The proposed tests use loads of 10–100 mN and sliding speeds of 0.1–1 m/s.
The proposed system uses a pure Cu substrate and either air or an inert-gas environment.
Below approximately 450 K, the coating has moderate stacking-fault energy.
Moderate stacking-fault energy enables stable dislocation glide and stacking-fault formation that accommodate strain without catastrophic failure.
Above approximately 450 K, the stacking-fault energy decreases significantly.
Reduced stacking-fault energy promotes widespread stacking-fault accumulation and dislocation dissociation.
Stacking-fault accumulation and dislocation dissociation cause loss of crystalline order and eventual amorphization.
Loss of crystalline order causes lattice softening, reduced elastic modulus, rapid material removal, and catastrophic wear.
Wear resistance remains stable up to approximately 450 K, with high elastic modulus and low wear rates.
Above 450 K, wear resistance declines sharply, elastic modulus drops significantly, and surface roughness increases.
At 300 K, FeNiCrCoCu coatings have stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus because of dislocation-mediated plasticity and stable stacking faults.
The approximately 450 K critical threshold is specific to FCC FeNiCrCoCu alloys having moderate stacking-fault energy.
The critical temperature can vary with composition, grain size, and processing history.
Stable wear above 450 K or a failure of stacking-fault energy to decrease with temperature would falsify the proposed mechanism.
